summary_corrections.erdos-hajnal-property-and-homogeneous-se:
The published clique and stable-set numbers of a finite graph, the notions of a hereditary class and of an $H$-free class, the complement of a graph and of a class, and the facts that complementation preserves hereditary classes and exchanges cliques with stable sets are the setting for what follows; induced embeddings compose. Finite Ramsey theory supplies the binomial bound on Ramsey numbers; the Erdős–Rényi random graph, the probability that a fixed pattern occurs, and the first-moment method supply the probabilistic counterpart; and the published theory of real powers and logarithms, including change of base and the fact that a logarithm grows more slowly than every positive power, is what makes $\log n$ and $n^{\epsilon}$ comparable.

A homogeneous set is a clique or a stable set, and $\operatorname{hom}(G)$ is the larger of the two numbers; a hereditary class has the Erdős–Hajnal property when some positive exponent $\epsilon$ forces $\operatorname{hom}(G)\ge|V(G)|^{\epsilon}$ throughout the class. The page proves that the admissible exponents are downward closed, that every nonempty $n$-vertex graph satisfies $\operatorname{hom}(G)\ge\tfrac12\log_2 n$, that $K_t$-free classes have the property and every $P_3$-free graph satisfies $\operatorname{hom}(G)\ge\sqrt{|V(G)|}$, and that for $n\ge16$ some $n$-vertex graph has $\operatorname{hom}(G)<3\log_2 n$, so the class of all graphs does not have the property. It then establishes complement invariance, passage to hereditary subclasses, monotonicity under induced pattern containment, the property for every graph on at most three vertices, and the equivalence of the single-pattern and finite-family formulations, closing with a remark stating the conjecture.
summary_corrections.regular-pairs-and-induced-counting:
A finite simple graph and its complement, the edges between two vertex sets and the pure and mixed pairs among them, an induced embedding, an induced copy of a fixed graph, the number of such copies, and what it means for a class of graphs to be hereditary are all published notions. From finite probability the development takes the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality for finite random variables, Markov's inequality, and the first-moment method; these are the inequalities behind the energy increment and behind every statement that all but a small fraction of vertices or pairs behave typically.

The page defines the edge density between two vertex sets and the $\epsilon$-regular pair, then makes that definition usable through typical degrees, slicing, complementation, and robustness under small edits. Regular and equitable partitions and the mean-square density, or energy, of a partition follow: energy is monotone under refinement, an irregularity witness forces a quantified energy boost, and iterating the increment proves the Szemerédi regularity lemma with an equitable partition, an explicit tower-type upper bound, and a refinement of any prescribed partition. Regular pairs then support triangle counting, counting copies of a fixed graph, and induced counting, which with edit distance give the graph removal lemma. Strong regularity by energy stabilisation, large self-regular subsets, the density-approximation lemma, and representative subsets carry the argument to the induced removal lemma, with a remark separating the tower and wowzer bounds.

summary_rationale.erdos-hajnal-property-and-homogeneous-se: Both paragraphs were the page's own development: paragraph 1 gave this page's definitions of a homogeneous set, hom(G) and the Erdős–Hajnal property together with items 3, 9, 11, 12 and 13, and paragraph 2 gave items 4, 7, 8 and 14. No declared dependency appeared as background anywhere. The proposal also set hom(G) in backticks, which is code formatting rather than mathematics. The replacement puts the published clique/stable-set numbers, hereditary and H-free classes, the complement dictionary, composition of induced embeddings, the Ramsey binomial bound, the Erdős–Rényi random graph with the fixed-pattern probability and the first-moment method, and the logarithm/real-power comparison in paragraph 1, and gives paragraph 2 the page's own progression in TeX.
summary_rationale.regular-pairs-and-induced-counting: Same failure: paragraph 1 opened with this page's own definition of an epsilon-regular pair and ran through items 4–12 without naming a single declared dependency. The replacement puts the published finite simple graph and complement, edges between sets with pure and mixed pairs, induced embeddings, induced copies and their number, hereditary classes, and the three probabilistic tools the energy argument actually uses — Cauchy–Schwarz for finite random variables, Markov's inequality, the first-moment method — in paragraph 1, and keeps the regularity-to-induced-removal development in paragraph 2. The tower-type bound is stated exactly as item 12 and item 24 state it, with no strengthening.
